title: Area under the curve by the trapezoidal rule

segs.text: Module one, objective five. The area under the curve, by the trapezoidal rule. A U C is the area under the plot of plasma concentration against time. It tells you the extent of drug that is available for the body to use: how much drug, not how fast. Its units are a concentration times a time, such as microgram hours per milliliter. There is rarely an equation for the curve, only a table of measured points, so the area is estimated from those points.

card.m: AUC: area under C<sub>p</sub> against time
AUC: extent of drug available (how much, not how fast)
table of points → estimate the area

segs.text: The trapezoidal rule joins each pair of neighbouring points with a straight line, which splits the area into strips. Each strip is a trapezoid, and its area is the average of its two concentrations times the time between them. She said, take this curve and break it up into little segments and then determine the area of each of those segments and add them up. The rule does not depend on the shape of the curve, so it works for any concentration time table, from any route. It does assume a straight line between points, so where the points are widely spaced on a curved stretch the estimate is less accurate, and the more points there are, the more accurate the area becomes.

card.m: straight line between points: wide spacing → more error; more points → more accurate

segs.text: The A U C of one segment equals C n minus one plus C n, over two, times t n minus t n minus one, where C n minus one and C n are the concentrations at the two ends of the segment. Adding the two concentrations and dividing by two averages those two heights, so the two is a plain number, not hours. The time difference is the width, read from the time column, so a wider strip or higher concentrations give a larger area. A concentration in micrograms per milliliter times a width in hours gives microgram hours per milliliter. A U C total is the sum of the A U C of every segment.

card.m: the 2 averages two heights; it is not hours
wider strip or higher C → larger area

segs.text: Her slide example gives plasma levels at six times, from half an hour to five hours, and asks for the A U C from hours two to four. The trapezoidal rule answers it, because only measured points are given. The first step is choosing the rows: only those inside two to four hours count, eighteen point four at two hours, eleven point one at three and six point seven seven at four, in micrograms per milliliter. The half hour and one hour rows are before the interval, and the five hour row is after it. That makes two segments, each one hour wide.

In her slide example, the strip from two to three hours has an area of eighteen point four plus eleven point one micrograms per milliliter, over two, times one hour: fourteen point seven five microgram hours per milliliter. The strip from three to four hours, from eleven point one to six point seven seven micrograms per milliliter, has an area of eight point nine three five microgram hours per milliliter, smaller because the concentrations are lower over the same width. The two areas add to twenty three point seven microgram hours per milliliter. This A U C is the extent of drug available between two and four hours only; the parts of the curve before two hours and after four hours would add more area.

Her questions give a table and an interval named in hours. Use only the trapezoids between rows inside that interval, not the whole table and not an extrapolated tail. Check each width from the time column: where sampling times are uneven, as from half an hour to one hour, a segment is half an hour wide, not one hour. When a student asked whether the two on the bottom of the trapezoid formula is hours, she said, No, two is not hours. Give the units as concentration times time, microgram hours per milliliter. A concept question asks what A U C tells you: the extent of drug available, how much, while how fast shows in the peak concentration, C max, and the time of the peak, t max.

A U C returns later in the course. Bioavailability, F, the fraction of an oral dose that enters the plasma, equals A U C oral over A U C I V. The oral area is on the top, so the smaller it is compared with the I V area, the smaller the fraction that entered the plasma. When the doses differ, the equation sheet corrects for them: F equals A U C p o over A U C I V, times D I V over D p o, where p o means by mouth. Clearance, the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time, also links the dose to the A U C, in Module two.

card.m: smaller AUC<sub>oral</sub> relative to AUC<sub>IV</sub> → smaller F
